title: Lt. Joseph P. O'Neil's Olympic expeditions, 1885 and 1890
status: complete first edition (2026-10-08). The 1890 report (Senate Doc. 59, 1896) and the 1907 participant accounts by Bretherton and Henderson were fetched and every quote from them was checked on page images. The 1885 report survives only in manuscript; its few quotes come from the NPS Historic Resource Study transcription. Wood's Men, Mules and Mountains was not read (in copyright); his facts reach us through his 1990 Columbia article and Evans's page citations. Verified 2026-10-08 (see VERIFY.md): every quote re-fetched and found verbatim in its public-domain source.
compiled_for: Olympic Peninsula Hiker (design stage). Part of the Robert L. Wood knowledge base: Wood's Men, Mules and Mountains (1976) is the standard history of these expeditions.
how_to_use: Facts in 'timeline', 'members', 'animals' and 'place_names' are in our own words. Each names the public-domain source we read ('sources') and, where Wood covers it, the Wood work to credit ('wood'). Keep a credit line such as 'After Robert L. Wood, Men, Mules and Mountains (1976)' wherever a Wood-sourced fact appears in game text.
'quote_pool' holds only verbatim lines from public-domain texts we fetched. Each has its page, URL and public-domain reason. Never add a line to it from memory or from a Wood book.

Quote text rules: copied letter-for-letter from the page image; straight ASCII quotes and apostrophes stand in for the printed curly ones; words split by a line-end hyphen are rejoined; the original spellings are kept ([sic] 'hurculean', 'Quinaiult', 'Brotherton'). 'excerpt': true means the quote is a contiguous part of a longer sentence.

For the death screen: pick from quote_pool by 'epitaph_fit' (fall, drowning, river, hypothermia, rain, starvation, exhaustion, lost, insects, bear, poison, avalanche, injury, fire, stuck, night, summit, scenery, memorial, survived, generic). Show the speaker and short source, e.g. '- Lt. Joseph P. O'Neil, report of 1890'. This answers the 'random Robert Wood sentence' request lawfully: Wood's own sentences cannot be used without permission, but the explorers' words he built his book on can.
'node_confidence' in the timeline: high = the source names the place; medium = strong inference from the route; low = a stand-in node near unidentified ground; none = no node fits.

copyright_policy.rule: No Robert L. Wood text is in this file. Wood's works are cited for facts only, restated in our own words.

expeditions.name: O'Neil's 1885 reconnaissance (Department of the Columbia)
expeditions.end: recalled from the mountains; sailed from Port Angeles Aug. 26
expeditions.authorized_by: Gen. Nelson A. Miles, commanding the Department of the Columbia (order signed by Asst. Adj. Gen. H. Clay Wood)
expeditions.goal_own_words: Look over the unknown country south of Port Angeles: what it was like, what it held, and how troops might cross it.
expeditions.route_own_words: A mule trail cut south from Port Angeles up the Ennis Creek country to the Mount Angeles - Klahhane Ridge heights ('The Sisters', with 'Victors Pass'), then over the first ridge and along the high divide south and east (Hurricane Ridge - Obstruction Point - Grand/Lillian ridges) to a last camp O'Neil called Noplace, probably in Cameron Basin. One side party tried the Elwha. O'Neil and Pvt. Johnson pushed on foot toward the Mount Anderson country before a courier recalled O'Neil to Fort Leavenworth.
expeditions.party_size: O'Neil says eight men and eight pack animals (SDOC59 p.17); Hanna (1907) says a party of seven men; Evans lists seven besides O'Neil plus, later, a Native guide/packer and a Mr. Pilcher.

expeditions.name: The Olympic Exploring Expedition, 1890 (U.S. Army and Oregon Alpine Club)
expeditions.start: Vancouver Barracks; landed at the mouth of Lilliwaup Creek, Hood Canal, July 2, 1890
expeditions.authorized_by: Gen. John Gibbon, commanding the Department of the Columbia (O'Neil named the main range the Gibbon Range for him)
expeditions.goal_own_words: Cross the range east to west from Hood Canal to the Pacific, cutting one main mule trail while small parties branched off to map the rivers on either side; the Oregon Alpine Club also wanted its copper box left on the summit of Mount Olympus.
expeditions.route_own_words: Lilliwaup - Lake Cushman (rafted across) - up the North Fork Skokomish past the copper miners' camp and a bluff the men bridged (the Staircase area) - Jumbo's Leap canyon - camps 6 to 9 up the North Fork - over the Skokomish-Duckabush divide (First Divide) - down into the upper Duckabush and up its main fork - Camp 14 at the foot of Mount Anderson on the Duckabush-Quinault divide (the O'Neil Pass country) - a 3,000-foot zigzag mule trail down to Camp 15 in the East Fork Quinault (Enchanted Valley) - down the East Fork to the forks and Lake Quinault - Humptulips City - Hoquiam Landing. Foot parties explored the South Fork Skokomish, Satsop, Wynoochee, Wishkah, Duckabush, Dosewallips, Humptulips, North Fork Quinault, Queets and the south side of Mount Olympus.
expeditions.trail_length: about 93 miles, Hood Canal to Grays Harbor; the Hoquiam Board of Trade cut about 30 miles of it (SDOC59 p.2). Mules made the whole trip in nine days once it was open (p.19).

timeline.event: O'Neil, a young 14th Infantry lieutenant at Fort Townsend, stares at the Olympics across the water and finds that nobody can tell him anything reliable about the interior.
After a transfer to Vancouver Barracks, O'Neil talks Gen. Nelson A. Miles into an exploration; the order is signed by Asst. Adj. Gen. H. Clay Wood.

The party leaves Port Angeles (then about forty people, a hotel, a sawmill and two stores) heading south into the foothills: up the Ennis Creek country (Evans), on a line much like today's Hurricane Ridge Road (NPS). Their Native guide leaves them the first night. It takes about a month to reach Hurricane Ridge.
timeline.node_note: Modern trailheads south of Port Angeles stand in for the 1885 line; the exact route is reconstructed.
game_hooks: The Native guide's departure must be told plainly and only after review with the Lower Elwha Klallam Tribe (see indigenous_notes).

timeline.event: Cutting trail toward a peak O'Neil called Mount Sherman (now Mount Angeles), the party crosses the first ridge by a pass near the peak ('Victors Pass') to the head of a stream they call Hawgood Creek. O'Neil's compass needle swings near a body of magnetic iron.
timeline.node_note: victor_pass shares its name with O'Neil's 'Victors Pass' on this route; we have not confirmed the modern pass is the same notch or that the name comes from 1885.

timeline.event: At the foot of the first snowy range. Long days on thin rations; mules keep tumbling off the steep sidehills.
From the heights O'Neil called The Sisters (Mount Angeles and Klahhane Ridge) he looks south over a wild jumble of peaks and takes one cluster for Mount Olympus.

On Hurricane Ridge the party splits. Engineer Harry Hawgood's group heads down toward the Elwha but loses its supplies in a river crossing and turns back; O'Neil's group follows the high divide south and east. Elk and deer are everywhere and the open ridges have little brush.

The mules stop at a camp O'Neil names Noplace, probably in Cameron Basin. O'Neil and Pvt. John Johnson go on foot toward the Mount Anderson country, get separated, and Johnson walks out alone. O'Neil locates and names Mount Claywood (for H. Clay Wood).
A courier brings orders sending O'Neil to Fort Leavenworth, Kansas. He sails from Port Angeles with the work unfinished. He later writes that the hardships were worth it.

Back in the Northwest from 1887, O'Neil becomes secretary of the new Oregon Alpine Club (Portland, founded 1887 by William G. Steel and others). The club and the Army agree on a joint expedition: the club pays most costs and sends three scientists; Gen. John Gibbon supplies O'Neil, soldiers, a packer, mules and dogs.
O'Neil leaves Vancouver Barracks for Puget Sound to prepare. He has the Seattle Press party's report (published July 16) in mind and thinks a winter crossing was a mistake.

The pack train leaves Vancouver Barracks under Sgt. Marsh with packer Price and Pvt. Barnes; the rest follow on the 25th and reach Fort Townsend on the 27th. The hired steamer Enterprise has burst her boilers, so the steamer Louise of Port Hadlock is chartered.

Overnight run down Hood Canal. No dock at the mouth of Lilliwaup Creek: boats ferry the supplies to the beach and the mules are pushed off the deck to swim. The trail to Lake Cushman, sold to them as good and six miles long, is steep, wet and choked with windfall. Henderson walks ahead alone, botanizing, and needs ten and a half hours. The main party camps in a swamp at 9 p.m. after about 2.5 miles; one mule wedges under a log and has to be cut out.
game_hooks: Opening scene option: mules swimming ashore in the rain.

timeline.event: Lake Cushman reached at noon. Everything is ferried over on settler Rose's old raft, and camp is made in Mr. Windoffer's field on the west shore. The night before, the advance party at the lake had almost nothing to eat until foragers brought bacon and bread and O'Neil walked in with a full haversack; the first mules straggled in at 6 p.m. on the 3rd.
place_names_then: Lake Cushman (natural lake, about 1.5 miles long in 1890)
timeline.node_note: The 1890 lake was far smaller than today's reservoir (dammed in the 1920s); staircase_trailhead at the head of the modern lake is the nearest node.

timeline.event: Independence Day off duty. The men fish; Henderson lands about a hundred trout in a few hours.
Scouts look for a way up the Skokomish while O'Neil finds a better supply trail from Hoodsport. Settler Frederic Church joins as a volunteer woodsman. It rains without letup.

Trail cut about 4.5 miles to Camp 2, near a camp of copper miners (the end of any existing trail). A bluff at the river's edge blocks the way, so the men fell trees against its face and cover them with dirt and boughs to make a mule ledge; it takes four and a half days. Krause, crippled by rheumatism, is relieved on July 8.
timeline.node_note: Wood names the cliff Fisher's Bluff. The Staircase name is commonly tied to this bridged bluff; we have not re-verified that link today (see uncertain).

timeline.event: Trail reaches Camp 3, about 7 miles above the lake. Trying to travel up the riverbed instead of chopping through windfall nearly drowns two mules and loses their loads; the crew goes back to the axe.

Henderson and Pvt. Fisher climb a high peak west of Lake Cushman (probably Mount Lincoln) and see Hood Canal, Mount Rainier and, far to the northwest, Olympus. They stumble back into camp at 9:30 p.m.
timeline.date_note: Henderson climbed on a rest day, sorted plants the next day, and broke camp at 8 a.m. on July 15, so the climb was about July 13. O'Neil does not date it.
timeline.node_note: Mount Lincoln has no node; the Flapjack Lakes - Gladys Divide country is the nearest playable high ground.

timeline.event: Camp 4 is set in a little basin about a mile below the falls, at the foot of the Canyon. Henderson calls it the point where the serious work begins.
timeline.date_note: O'Neil: Camp 4 established July 14. Henderson: reached at 9 a.m. July 15.

timeline.event: Scouting parties fan out. Henderson, Linsley and Sgt. Yates go up the South Branch, followed against their wishes by the hound Jumbo, who wins them over. They sleep by a fire on a 30-degree slope with no blankets and melt snow for tea. Another party reaches 'Bruins Peak' and first sees the East Fork Quinault; two visiting hunters who came along never ask to join again.

A box canyon only about 80 feet wide and deep stops the mules near Camp 5. Scouts cross by swinging on a tree; the pack train needs nearly a week of bridge-building. The men name it Jumbo's Leap. A mule rolls down the canyon side and is badly hurt.
timeline.node_note: Jumbo's Leap and Five Stream have no nodes. O'Neil says the Wickersham party passed 'Camp 5'; Evans puts that meeting at O'Neil's camp on Five Stream, so Camp 5 / Jumbo's Leap were probably near Five Stream (our inference).
game_hooks: Wood (COL1990) explains the name: the old dog Jumbo went into the canyon sooner than stay behind. O'Neil's report does not explain the name.

timeline.event: Judge James Wickersham's family party (sponsored by the Buckley Banner) passes the camp, bound for Port Angeles; they end up descending the Dosewallips to Hood Canal after hard going. O'Neil later hears that one of them was badly poisoned.

Church and Bretherton set out to map the South Fork Skokomish on short rations (three days' worth per O'Neil; Henderson says five on one page and three on the next). It takes them well over a week, the last days nearly foodless; hunters from Olympia help them out.
timeline.date_note: Henderson: gone since July 18. O'Neil: sent from Camp 5, trip took fifteen days. Henderson: seven or eight days.

timeline.event: Dr. J. Church (a physician just out from Washington, D.C.) joins the party.

Camp 6 above the falls (July 27) and Camp 7 by a big snowbank at only 2,300 feet (July 28). Henderson slashes his wrist cutting fir boughs for bedding. Scouts report the line is impossible for mules; everyone falls back to Camp 6 by July 30.

Three scouting parties leave Camp 6 in a downpour with orders not to return until their routes prove impossible or safe. On Aug. 3 Henderson heads home with Pvt. Higgins and the mule Frenchy, leaving his plant press with Pvt. Fisher.

After nine days out, Sgts. Marsh and Yates and Pvt. Fisher return: a route goes up the North Fork to its head, over a divide into an unknown valley (it proves to be the Duckabush). They kill several elk; until then the only fresh meat had been a deer or a bear shot by earlier scouts. All hands move to the new line.

Camp 9 is reached, about 5 miles below the head of the North Fork and 2 miles below the divide. From here small parties are sent out while the rest push the mule trail on. O'Neil warns of poisonous 'stagger weed' where the mules graze.
timeline.node_note: Camp 9 is where the trail left the river to climb to the divide; that fits the stretch below First Divide (Nine Stream - Two Bear). Whether the stream name 'Nine Stream' comes from Camp 9 is unverified.

timeline.event: Foot parties depart. Church and Dr. Church head for the Satsop, Wynoochee and Wishkah; Bretherton and Sgt. Yates for the Duckabush and Dosewallips; O'Neil with Pvts. Fisher and Danton for the East Fork Quinault, Lake Quinault and the Humptulips.

O'Neil's party leaves at 5:30 a.m. with 50 lb each, hauls up 2,500 feet by huckleberry bushes, inches along a slate ledge for an hour and a half, and at 5 p.m. tops the Quinault divide to see the snowy main range. Going down, a broad elk trail ends at a cliff; they spend the night in a gully. Next morning Danton nearly falls from a ledge. By noon they reach the East Fork Quinault, which heads under Mount Anderson's glaciers.
timeline.node_note: We do not know where they crossed; the descent ended at the upper East Fork Quinault, the Enchanted Valley reach.

timeline.event: Five hard days down the Quinault to the lake, a few hours as guests of a settler, then three days to Humptulips City ('two houses and a name') and twelve days on the Humptulips and Hoquiam rivers.

The side parties suffer: Church falls on a Satsop bluff, ruins his compass and loses food, and he and the doctor live on berries for five days (the doctor tries shoe leather); Bretherton and Yates trace the Duckabush and Dosewallips to Hood Canal.

At Hoquiam the Board of Trade offers to cut a trail from town to meet the expedition's if O'Neil will use it (done by Sept. 25). He goes back by steamer and rail to Union City and walks his own trail to camp in three days.

Linsley and Sgt. Marsh with eight men finish the trail to the foot of Mount Anderson and bring up all supplies. At Camp 14, on the Duckabush-Quinault divide, they report that the mules can go no farther.
timeline.node_note: O'Neil's trail directions (p.20) climb the Duckabush main fork to the Duckabush-Quinault divide and drop into the Quinault: the O'Neil Pass line. Evans: the trail circled north of Mount Steel to O'Neil Pass. The exact site of Camp 14 is not given in the report.

timeline.event: All parties are back in camp. Everyone is sent out to look for a way down.

A route is found, and a zigzag mule trail is built down about 3,000 feet into the East Fork Quinault, nearly five miles of trail to make three-quarters of a mile. Camp 15 is made on the Quinault side. Extra gear goes back: each man keeps one blanket, half a shelter tent, spare socks and underwear. A month of food is kept.
timeline.date_note: O'Neil writes that the search took thirteen days, which does not fit his own Sept. 6 and Sept. 16 dates; Bretherton's party left 'headquarters' on Sept. 13.
timeline.node_note: Wood (COL1990) identifies the pass the scouts found as the one later named O'Neil Pass.

timeline.event: Yellow-jackets infest the north slope of the Skokomish-Duckabush divide. Fires set to burn the nests spread over the trail. Two mules roll more than 100 feet and are left; Sgt. Marsh forces the pack train through the burning hillside to Hoodsport for stores and back. (One of the abandoned mules, B. C., later died near Lake Cushman; the other died at Hoodsport.)
timeline.node_note: The divide runs between the North Fork Skokomish (south) and the Duckabush (north), so its north slope is the drop from First Divide toward Home Sweet Home.
game_hooks: A wasp-nest hazard at First Divide is historically grounded.

timeline.event: The Linsley party (Linsley, Bretherton, Sgt. Yates, Pvts. Fisher, Danton, Kranichfeld, Hughes) leaves with 25 days' food: find the Elwha's source, place the Oregon Alpine Club's copper box on Olympus, then explore the Hoh and Quillayute. First night: a creek they name Fire Creek 'on account of a slight accident'; next day yellow-jackets on the climb to the divide.
timeline.date_note: Bretherton: left Sept. 13. O'Neil: orders given Sept. 16.
timeline.node_note: Bretherton says they followed the East Fork's right bank down to a stream from the north; today's Fire Creek is a north-side tributary. Whether the modern name descends from 1890 is unconfirmed.

timeline.event: They cross into the Elwha headwaters, camp on a park-like saddle they name Bretherton's Pass, lose a day to fog, cross a 5,500-foot ridge (Sept. 17) and reach the Elwha above its forks, where they find a joke poem left at an old camp.
timeline.node_note: Bretherton's Pass has not been identified with a modern name; do not label any node with it.

timeline.event: Up a long glacier to the head of the Queets; across 'Pluto's Gulch' to a flowery plateau they call the Garden of the Gods. Pvt. Fisher is separated in an alder thicket; that night they see his fire far below from a camp on the edge of a 5,200-foot drop.
timeline.node_note: Evans: the party went from O'Neil Pass northwest to the Queets Basin and up to the head of Jeffers Glacier.

timeline.event: Linsley, Bretherton and Danton climb to a summit of Mount Olympus from the south and leave the copper box (with a record book and trinkets: a pencil, a glove from the Wickersham party, cards, army buttons, a beer check, shoelaces, a visiting card, three cablegrams). Wood judged it probably a crag of the South Peak, not the true top. The box has never been found. O'Neil believed no one had stood there before (i.e., first recorded by settlers).
timeline.node_note: Their summit was on the south side; mount_olympus_west_peak is only a stand-in for 'Olympus'. Do not claim the West Peak was climbed in 1890.

timeline.event: Fisher gives up trying to rejoin and follows the Queets to the ocean. Short of boots and food, Linsley also takes the Queets instead of the assigned Hoh and Quillayute (thinking at first it was the Hoh), passes the Quinault agency on Sept. 29 and goes on to Hoquiam. O'Neil is not pleased.
game_hooks: Wood (COL1990) notes Native people helped the lone man on the lower Queets; any portrayal needs review with the Quinault Indian Nation.

timeline.event: The pack train descends from the divide into the East Fork Quinault ('like flies coming down a wall') and makes the forks in about five days. Just past the dangerous canyon, yellow-jackets stampede the mules; one leaps the bluff and dies on a ledge 200 feet down with the coffee and O'Neil's papers. The mule Sorais also rolled into the Quinault gorge (the report does not say when).
timeline.node_note: The deadly 'canyon' is somewhere on the East Fork above the forks; the Pony Bridge gorge is a plausible stand-in, not a confirmed site.

timeline.event: The pack train is sent out to Hoquiam on the Board of Trade trail. O'Neil, Frederic Church, Dr. Church and a Mr. West head for the head of the North Fork Quinault, finding many old Seattle Press camps; Sgt. Marsh and McCarty cross toward the Humptulips.

Canyon Creek gorge in the rain; a view of the Queets and of Olympus 'with its forty glaciers'. Church and the doctor go down the Queets; O'Neil and West look for the Raft River, take a bad tumble (one broken finger, the worst injury of the expedition), lose O'Neil's watch and food in a pool, and follow a stream that vanishes underground for three hours. O'Neil names it the West Branch.

At Lake Quinault after three days of rain, then two days by canoe down the Quinault River in the rain. A Quinault family takes O'Neil in for a night and feeds him; on Sept. 30 he reaches the Quinault agency at the river mouth.
game_hooks: O'Neil records his hosts' names and describes them in 1890 terms that are now offensive. Do not quote those passages; consult the Quinault Indian Nation before depicting this night at all.

timeline.event: O'Neil reaches Hoquiam on Oct. 1. The explorers are feted there (Oct. 4), disband (Oct. 6) and are given a banquet by the Oregon Alpine Club in Portland (Oct. 22).

O'Neil submits his report at Vancouver Barracks: the outer slopes are valuable, the interior is useless for settlement but would make a fine national park, chiefly to save the elk. He repeats the idea in a Portland lecture on Dec. 6.

At the request of UW president Mark W. Harrington, the report is printed as Senate Doc. 59 and referred to the Select Committee on Forest Reservations and the Protection of Game. The map, photographs and scientists' reports were not included.
Seventeen years on, The Mountaineers say they know nothing of what O'Neil's 1890 party accomplished; that summer Steel Points prints Bretherton's and Henderson's accounts.
Mount Olympus National Monument (1909) and Olympic National Park (June 29, 1938) follow; O'Neil, who rose to brigadier general, dies about four weeks after the park is created.

mules.name: B. C.
mules.fate: Gave out from cold and exposure and was left at a good camp (p.3); after rolling off the trail on the yellow-jacket hill he was abandoned and reached Lake Cushman, dying the day before Sgt. Marsh came to fetch him (p.13).

mules.name: Sorais
mules.fate: Fell from the trail into the gorge of the Quinault; no bones broken, but she could not be saved.

mules.name: Weakback
mules.fate: Stung by yellow-jackets, bolted over the precipice in the wildest part of the Quinault canyon (probably the mule whose neck broke on a ledge 200 feet down, carrying the coffee).

mules.name: Frenchy
mules.fate: Survived; the 'faithful little mule' that carried Henderson's plant collection out to Hoodsport on Aug. 3.

mules.name: (unnamed)
mules.fate: A second mule abandoned after the 100-foot fall on the yellow-jacket hill; brought to Hoodsport and died the next day. Another was badly hurt rolling down the canyon hill at Camp 5. Four were nearly drowned at a Skokomish ford until packer Price cut them free.

animals.mule_count_notes: About a dozen mules in 1890 (Evans, Wood). O'Neil's letter says three mules were the only casualties, but his narrative describes four deaths (B. C., the second abandoned mule, Sorais, and the mule that went over the bluff), unless Weakback and the bluff mule are counted twice. In 1885: eight pack animals.

dogs.name: Jumbo
dogs.what: An old mastiff-hound (Henderson). Unwanted on a scouting trip until 'famine, toil and heroism' won the men over. The box canyon Jumbo's Leap carries his name; Wood's account is that the dog went into the canyon sooner than stay behind.

dogs.name: (hounds)
dogs.what: Henderson heard 'the baying of hounds' in camp, so there was more than one dog.

epitaph_shortlist.note: Hand-picked lines that read well on a death screen, keyed by cause. All are in quote_pool with full citations. Grim mule lines (oq060, oq063) are left off; use them only if the tone fits.

indigenous_notes.principle: The country O'Neil crossed is the homeland of the Skokomish (Twana) people on the Hood Canal side and the Quinault on the Quinault River side; the 1885 route lies in Klallam country (today the Lower Elwha Klallam, Jamestown S'Klallam and Port Gamble S'Klallam tribes). The Park Service names eight tribes with ties to the park: Lower Elwha Klallam, Jamestown S'Klallam, Port Gamble S'Klallam, Skokomish, Quinault, Hoh, Quileute and Makah.
facts_in_the_record: 1885: a Native guide left O'Neil's party on its first night out of Port Angeles (Wood, COL1990 p.41); Evans also notes a Native guide and packer who joined later. Neither is named.
1890: O'Neil hired Native packers at times to carry supplies on schedule (SDOC59 p.3). They are not named.
1890: Pvt. Fisher, alone on the lower Queets, was helped by Native people (Wood, COL1990 p.45).
1890: a Quinault household sheltered and fed O'Neil for a night on the Quinault River (SDOC59 p.16), and the agency at Taholah gave him dry clothes and dinner.

O'Neil wrote that the rivers carry names given by the peoples living at their mouths, and he collected name translations and 'legends'; those appendices were not printed in 1896 and we have not seen them.
rules: Do not quote O'Neil's or Henderson's remarks about Native people (SDOC59 pp. 3, 11, 15-16; Steel Points p.191). They use 1890 language and judgments that are offensive and, in places, wrong (O'Neil predicted the Skokomish would soon be extinct; the Skokomish Indian Tribe is a living nation).
Do not retell or reconstruct any legend or name translation O'Neil gathered, and do not adapt the legend chapters of Wood's The Land That Slept Late.
Say 'first recorded' or 'first documented', never 'first ever': the explorers' claims to untrodden ground (e.g., oq077) reflect what settlers knew.

Before any scene shows a Native person from this record (the departing guide, the packers, the people who helped Fisher, O'Neil's Quinault hosts), consult the relevant nation: Lower Elwha Klallam Tribe (1885 route), Skokomish Indian Tribe (Lake Cushman, Skokomish valleys), Quinault Indian Nation (Quinault, Queets).
O'Neil recorded the names of his Quinault hosts; do not use those names in game text without the Quinault Indian Nation's agreement.

uncertain: Staircase place-name origin: commonly linked to the 1890 bridging of a river bluff near Camp 2 (and the wood_bibliography cites an NPS audio-tour page, now returning 404). Not confirmed against a current NPS or Board on Geographic Names source.
Whether 'Nine Stream' and the other numbered streams of the North Fork Skokomish relate to O'Neil's numbered camps: no source found.
Whether today's Fire Creek on the East Fork Quinault is the stream the Linsley party named in 1890: likely from Bretherton's description, unconfirmed.

Exact sites of Camps 5, 9, 14 and 15, Jumbo's Leap, Bruins Peak, Bretherton's Pass, Pluto's Gulch and the Garden of the Gods. Wood's maps in Men, Mules and Mountains would settle most of these; check before labeling nodes.
Which two upper-Duckabush lakes O'Neil named Francis and John.

Date conflicts: Camp 4 (O'Neil July 14, Henderson July 15); Linsley party departure (Bretherton Sept. 13, O'Neil Sept. 16); the 'thirteen days' search for the mule route; the pack train reaching the Quinault forks (O'Neil about Sept. 21-22, Wood Sept. 24).
Party sizes: 1885 'eight men' (O'Neil) vs 'seven men' (Hanna) vs Evans's list; 1890 name spellings (Barnes/Bairens, Haffner's rank).
The Olympus summit of Sept. 22, 1890: O'Neil gives 7,875 ft by aneroid, Bretherton 7,550 ft; Wood thought it a south-side crag, not the true summit.
O'Neil's 1885 report quotes depend on Evans's transcription (we did not see the manuscript).
Victor Pass: same notch and same name origin as O'Neil's 'Victors Pass'? Likely, not confirmed.
